concept.name: PostgreSQL Query Planner

relationships.description: Connects PostgreSQL Query Planner to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: The PostgreSQL query planner is a cost-based optimizer that estimates I/O and CPU work across candidate scan, join, and sort trees using table statistics (`pg_statistic`) to pick the lowest-cost execution plan.
spark.keyTakeaway: Bad plans almost always trace back to stale statistics, correlated columns, or miscalibrated cost parameters (`random_page_cost`, `work_mem`)—inspect `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before adding indexes.

concept.whyItMatters: A single misestimated row count in a 4-table join can flip PostgreSQL from a 3 ms Nested Loop with Index Scan to a 45-second Hash Join spilling hundreds of megabytes to disk. Understanding how the planner computes selectivity and costs lets you fix slow queries systematically rather than guessing at indexes.
whenToUse: Diagnosing why a query regressed from milliseconds to seconds after data growth or a PostgreSQL upgrade.
Tuning `work_mem`, `random_page_cost`, and `effective_cache_size` for NVMe SSDs vs. spinning disks.
Designing composite indexes, partial indexes, or `CREATE STATISTICS` objects for skewed or correlated columns.
whenNotToUse: When the bottleneck is lock contention (`pg_locks`), connection pool exhaustion, or vacuum bloat rather than the execution plan itself.
Micro-optimizing single-row primary-key lookups (`WHERE id = $1`) that already use `Index Scan` in under 0.2 ms.
Using planner-hint extensions like `pg_hint_plan` as a first resort before fixing stale `ANALYZE` stats or missing multi-column statistics.
keyPoints: PostgreSQL estimates row selectivity from `pg_statistic` (exposed via `pg_stats`): `null_frac`, `n_distinct`, `most_common_vals` (MCV), and equidepth histograms (default 100 buckets via `default_statistics_target`).

Total plan cost is measured in arbitrary units anchored to `seq_page_cost = 1.0`, `random_page_cost = 4.0` (often lowered to `1.1` on NVMe SSDs), and CPU tuple/operator constants (`cpu_tuple_cost = 0.01`).

The planner chooses among **Nested Loop** (fast for small outer sets + indexed inner), **Hash Join** (fast for medium/large unsorted sets fitting in `work_mem`), and **Merge Join** (fast for large pre-sorted or B-tree-indexed inputs).

Independent-column assumptions fail on correlated predicates like `WHERE city = 'Bengaluru' AND state = 'Karnataka'`, causing severe underestimates until you add `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies, mcv)`.
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reveals the truth: compare `rows=` (estimated) vs. `actual rows=` and watch `shared read` vs. `temp read/written` blocks.

examples.title: Fixing a Hash Join disk spill with `work_mem`
examples.scenario: An analytics query joining 1.2M `orders` with 300K `customers` takes 4.8 seconds. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows `Hash Batches: 32  Memory Usage: 4097kB` and `temp read=44210 written=44298` because default `work_mem = 4MB` is too small for the hash table.
examples.outcome: Setting `SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB'` for that reporting session keeps the entire hash table in RAM (`Hash Batches: 1`), dropping execution time from 4,800 ms to 390 ms.

examples.title: Correlated columns fixed by Extended Statistics
examples.scenario: A query filters `WHERE country = 'IN' AND currency = 'INR'` on a 20M-row `transactions` table. Assuming independence, the planner multiplies `0.08 * 0.08 = 0.0064`, estimates 128K rows instead of the actual 1.6M rows, and picks a catastrophic Nested Loop.
examples.outcome: Running `CREATE STATISTICS tx_country_currency (dependencies, mcv) ON country, currency FROM transactions; ANALYZE transactions;` corrects the estimate to 1.58M rows, switching the plan to a Hash Join and cutting latency from 14.2 s to 620 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: More MCV entries and finer histograms dramatically improve selectivity estimates on skewed data.
tradeOffs.con: `ANALYZE` takes longer, `pg_statistic` grows, and the planner spends slightly more CPU per query parsing larger histograms.

tradeOffs.pro: Encourages the planner to use Index Scans and Bitmap Index Scans instead of conservative Sequential Scans on modern NVMe storage.
tradeOffs.con: Can occasionally pick an Index Scan over a Seq Scan on a table with very poor physical clustering (low correlation).

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates external merge sorts (`Sort Method: external merge Disk`) and multi-batch Hash Joins.
tradeOffs.con: `work_mem` is allocated *per sort/hash node per connection*, so setting it too high globally risks OOM under 200 concurrent connections.

failureModes.name: Stale statistics after bulk loads
failureModes.description: Inserting 5M rows into a table before `autovacuum` runs `ANALYZE` leaves `reltuples` near zero, tricking the planner into choosing Nested Loops over millions of rows.
failureModes.mitigation: Run explicit `ANALYZE table_name;` immediately after bulk `COPY` or batch ETL loads, and lower `autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor` (e.g., `0.02`) on huge tables.

failureModes.name: Parameter sniffing / generic plan trap
failureModes.description: After 5 executions of a prepared statement, PostgreSQL (`plan_cache_mode = auto`) may switch to a cached generic plan whose average-case cost looks cheaper than a custom plan, hurting skewed tenant IDs.
failureModes.mitigation: Inspect with `EXPLAIN` on prepared statements; for heavily skewed multi-tenant queries, set `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` at the session or role level.

failureModes.name: Non-sargable predicates hiding indexes
failureModes.description: Writing `WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-12'` or `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'` prevents the planner from using a standard B-tree index on the raw column.
failureModes.mitigation: Rewrite as half-open range `created_at >= '2026-11-12' AND created_at < '2026-11-13'` or create an expression index `ON users (LOWER(email))`.

failureModes.name: Index Only Scan degrading to heap fetches
failureModes.description: An `Index Only Scan` still hits the table heap for every row if the visibility map isn't updated, showing high `Heap Fetches` in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.
failureModes.mitigation: Tune `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` on write-heavy tables so `VACUUM` marks pages all-visible in the visibility map.

commonMistakes: Running `EXPLAIN` without `ANALYZE, BUFFERS`, seeing only planner guesses instead of actual row counts and I/O blocks.
Leaving `random_page_cost = 4.0` and `effective_cache_size = 4GB` at defaults on a 64 GB RAM NVMe production server.
Adding a new index for every slow query without checking if `ANALYZE` was stale or if an existing composite index column order was reversed.
Setting global `work_mem = 256MB` with `max_connections = 500` and wondering why the Linux OOM killer terminates Postgres.
Wrapping indexed columns in functions (`COALESCE(col, '')`, `col::text`) in `WHERE` clauses, forcing Sequential Scans.

sections.content:
## The idea

SQL is declarative: you describe *what* rows you want, not *how* to fetch them. The PostgreSQL query planner bridges that gap using a **cost-based optimizer (CBO)**. Given a parsed and rewritten query tree, it generates equivalent physical execution trees—varying scan methods (`Seq Scan`, `Index Scan`, `Bitmap Heap Scan`), join algorithms (`Nested Loop`, `Hash Join`, `Merge Join`), and join orders—and scores each one.

Every score is a weighted sum of estimated disk I/O (`seq_page_cost`, `random_page_cost`) and CPU work (`cpu_tuple_cost`, `cpu_operator_cost`), driven by row-count estimates derived from `pg_statistic`. Because cost formulas are deterministic, poor plans almost always mean the planner's *row-count model* diverges from reality.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider `SELECT o.id, c.tier FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'PENDING' AND o.created_at >= now() - interval '1 day';` on 10M `orders` and 500K `customers`:

1. **Parse & rewrite**: PostgreSQL parses the SQL into a `Query` tree and expands any views or rules.
2. **Selectivity estimation**: Using `pg_stats` on `orders`, the planner checks the MCV list for `status = 'PENDING'` (say `0.02` of rows) and the histogram for `created_at` (say `0.005` of rows). Assuming independence, it estimates $10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.02 \times 0.005 = 1{,}000$ matching orders.
3. **Scan selection**: With `random_page_cost = 1.1`, scanning ~1,000 rows via a composite index `(status, created_at)` costs ~1,200 units, beating a full 140,000-page `Seq Scan` (~140,000 units).
4. **Join enumeration**: For 1,000 outer `orders` rows, a `Nested Loop` probing the primary key index `customers_pkey` 1,000 times costs less than hashing all 500K `customers` rows. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` confirms `actual rows=984` and completes in `4.1 ms`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Join strategies: Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join
sections.content:
## Join strategies: Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join

PostgreSQL chooses among three physical join operators based on input cardinalities, sort order, and `work_mem`:

- **Nested Loop**: Iterates over the outer relation and probes the inner relation (usually via an Index Scan) for each row. Optimal when the outer set is small (tens to low thousands of rows) and the inner join key is indexed.
- **Hash Join**: Builds an in-memory hash table of the smaller relation (up to `work_mem`) and streams the larger relation once to probe it. Optimal for medium-to-large unsorted equi-joins; degrades sharply if `work_mem` forces multi-batch disk spills.
- **Merge Join**: Scans two inputs already sorted on the join key (via B-tree index or explicit `Sort`) in a single linear pass. Optimal for very large datasets or non-equi-free pre-sorted streams that would overflow `work_mem` in a Hash Join.

## PostgreSQL scan methods compared

| Scan Type | How It Reads | Optimal Selectivity | Key Requirement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sequential Scan** | Reads every heap page in order | > 15–25% of table (or tiny tables) | High sequential I/O throughput |
| **Index Scan** | Traverses B-tree, fetches heap tuples | < 1–5% of table | Selective predicate on leading index columns |
| **Index Only Scan** | Reads B-tree leaf pages; skips heap | < 5–10% of table | Covering columns (`INCLUDE`) + clean visibility map |
| **Bitmap Heap Scan** | Collects TIDs in bitmap, sorts by page | 2–20% of table (or `OR` / multi-index) | Fits in `work_mem`; avoids random heap thrashing |

## Failure modes

Four recurring patterns cause the PostgreSQL planner to pick catastrophic plans:

1. **Correlated predicates**: Filtering on two dependent columns (`make = 'Toyota' AND model = 'Camry'`) without `CREATE STATISTICS` causes multiplicative underestimation ($P(A) \times P(B)$).
2. **CTE optimization fences (pre-PG 12) or `OFFSET` traps**: Deep `OFFSET 500000` still scans and discards 500,000 rows; replace with keyset pagination (`WHERE id > $last_id LIMIT 50`).
3. **`LIMIT` optimism**: A query with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10` and a rare `WHERE` filter may tempt the planner into scanning the `created_at` index backward, hitting millions of non-matching rows before finding 10.
4. **Bloat distorting `relpages`**: Dead tuples inflate table and index page counts, raising scan costs and slowing I/O even when live row counts are small.

## High-leverage configuration parameters

Start tuning at the cluster and session level before rewriting every query:

- **`random_page_cost = 1.1`** (down from `4.0`) and **`effective_io_concurrency = 200`** on NVMe SSDs.
- **`effective_cache_size`**: Set to ~75% of total system RAM (shared_buffers + OS page cache) so the planner knows index pages are likely cached.
- **`work_mem`**: Keep modest globally (e.g., `16MB`–`32MB` depending on `max_connections` via PgBouncer), and bump per-session (`SET LOCAL work_mem = '128MB'`) for heavy analytical reports.
- **`jit = off`** for OLTP workloads: LLVM JIT compilation (enabled by default in PG 12+ above `jit_above_cost = 100000`) can add 50–150 ms of compile overhead to medium OLTP queries.

## Practical checklist

- Always diagnose with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and inspect the *first* node where `estimated rows` differs from `actual rows` by > 10x.
- Set `random_page_cost = 1.1` and `effective_cache_size` accurately for your SSD hardware.
- Create `CREATE STATISTICS` (`dependencies`, `mcv`) whenever `WHERE` clauses filter on correlated columns.
- Run `ANALYZE` immediately after bulk data loads and monitor `pg_stat_user_tables.n_mod_since_analyze`.
- Watch `temp written` in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and tune `work_mem` per-session for batch jobs.

interviewProblems.title: PostgreSQL Query Planner
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on PostgreSQL Query Planner. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The PostgreSQL query planner is a cost-based optimizer that estimates I/O and CPU work across candidate scan, join, and sort trees using table statistics (`pg_statistic`) to pick the lowest-cost execution plan.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Cost-Based Planner applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Plan Executor.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Plan Executor experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Run explicit `ANALYZE table_name;` immediately after bulk `COPY` or batch ETL loads, and lower `autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor` (e.g., `0.02`) on huge tables.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Bad plans almost always trace back to stale statistics, correlated columns, or miscalibrated cost parameters (`random_page_cost`, `work_mem`)—inspect `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before adding indexes.
Avoid trap: Running `EXPLAIN` without `ANALYZE, BUFFERS`, seeing only planner guesses instead of actual row counts and I/O blocks.
Avoid trap: Leaving `random_page_cost = 4.0` and `effective_cache_size = 4GB` at defaults on a 64 GB RAM NVMe production server.
When to reach for it: Diagnosing why a query regressed from milliseconds to seconds after data growth or a PostgreSQL upgrade.
When to reach for it: Tuning `work_mem`, `random_page_cost`, and `effective_cache_size` for NVMe SSDs vs. spinning disks.

putItTogether.title: Putting Postgresql Query Planner Together
putItTogether.summary: Bad plans almost always trace back to stale statistics, correlated columns, or miscalibrated cost parameters (`random_page_cost`, `work_mem`)—inspect `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before adding indexes.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Postgresql Query Planner before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Setting `SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB'` for that reporting session keeps the entire hash table in RAM (`Hash Batches: 1`), dropping execution time from 4,800 ms to 390 ms.
